To negotiate means to have a back-and-forth discussion with one or more people in order to reach an agreement that everyone can accept — especially when those people have different or conflicting interests.

Think of it this way: you want one thing, the other person wants something else, and neither of you can simply force the other to give in. So instead of fighting or walking away, you talk it through, offer things, ask for things, and eventually land on a middle ground that works for both of you. That whole process is negotiating.
What Makes It "Negotiating" — and Not Just Talking?

Not every conversation is a negotiation. Three things define it:

1. There are competing interests. Both sides want something, and those wants don't perfectly match. A buyer wants to pay less; a seller wants to earn more. An employee wants a higher salary; a company wants to keep costs low.

2. Both sides have some power. Neither side can simply dictate to the other. If one side can just force the other, there's nothing to negotiate — it's a command. True negotiation only happens when both sides have something the other needs.

3. The goal is a mutual agreement. You're not just arguing. You're working toward a deal. Each side gives something up and gains something in return. This is called a compromise, and it's the usual result of successful negotiation.

"Negotiate" appears in many different areas of life:

In business: Companies negotiate contracts, prices, and deals. "The two companies negotiated a partnership agreement."

In the workplace: Employees negotiate salaries and benefits with employers. "She negotiated a 15% pay raise before accepting the job offer."

In international affairs: Countries negotiate peace treaties, trade agreements, and diplomatic deals. "The two nations negotiated a ceasefire after months of conflict."

In everyday life: Even informal situations count. "The children negotiated over who would get the last slice of pizza." Or: "He negotiated with his landlord to lower the rent."

In legal settings: Lawyers negotiate settlements — agreements reached before a case goes to trial. "The two parties negotiated a settlement out of court."

"Negotiate" also has a second sense that is completely different from agreements and deals. It means to successfully navigate or get through a physical obstacle or difficult situation — usually by handling it with skill and care.

Examples:

  • "The driver carefully negotiated the narrow mountain road." (= steered through it skillfully)
  • "She negotiated the crowded market without bumping into anyone." (= moved through it successfully)
  • "The pilot negotiated the severe storm and landed safely." (= managed through a difficult situation)

In this sense, the "obstacle" takes the place of the "other party," and successfully getting past it takes the place of "reaching a deal." The common thread is: something difficult stood in the way, and you handled it skillfully.

Understanding what negotiation is not makes the meaning much sharper:

  • It is not demanding. Demanding means you simply state what you want and expect the other person to comply. Negotiating means you're open to discussion and compromise.
  • It is not begging. Begging means asking from a position of no power. Negotiating means you have something to offer in return.
  • It is not forcing. If you force someone, there's no discussion. Negotiating requires willingness from both sides.
  • It is not a one-sided conversation. It always involves at least two parties exchanging offers, ideas, or positions.

What truly defines "negotiate" is the spirit of finding middle ground. Both parties come with their own needs, but they respect that the other side has needs too. They talk, they listen, they make offers, they adjust, and they move toward each other — not away. The goal is always an agreement that both sides can live with, even if it's not the perfect outcome for either.

Since you want full mastery of this word, here are its closest relatives:

  • Negotiation (noun) — the process or act of negotiating. "The negotiation lasted three days."
  • Negotiator (noun) — a person who negotiates, especially professionally. "She is a skilled negotiator."
  • Negotiable (adjective) — able to be changed through negotiation; open to discussion. "The price is negotiable." (Its opposite is non-negotiable — meaning it cannot be changed or debated.)
  • Negotiated (past tense / adjective) — "They reached a negotiated settlement."
Common Phrases You'll Hear With This Word

• Negotiate a deal — to work out and agree on a deal
  • Negotiate a contract — to discuss and agree on the terms of a contract
  • Negotiate terms — to discuss the specific conditions of an agreement
  • Negotiate in good faith — to negotiate honestly, with a genuine intention to reach an agreement (not to deceive)
  • Negotiate a raise — to discuss and persuade an employer to increase your salary
  • Hard to negotiate with — describing someone who is stubborn or inflexible in discussions

To negotiate means: to engage in a deliberate, mutual discussion with someone who has different interests, with the aim of reaching an agreement both parties can accept — and less commonly, to skillfully handle or move through a physical obstacle or challenge.
